concepts.definition: Opens the serial port and sets the communication speed (baud). These lessons always use 9600.
concepts.example: You write Serial.begin(9600); inside setup(), and the monitor is set to 9600 as well.
concepts.pitfall: Choosing different speeds in the code and in the monitor: the screen fills with meaningless characters.

concepts.definition: print leaves the text on the same line; println writes and moves to the next line.
concepts.example: Serial.print("D2 = "); Serial.println(1); writes D2 = 1 on a single line on the screen.
concepts.pitfall: Always using print and being surprised that all the output joins up on one line.

concepts.definition: available() gives the number of bytes waiting to be read; read() reads one byte from the buffer.
concepts.example: if (Serial.available() > 0) { char c = Serial.read(); } first checks whether there is any data.
concepts.pitfall: Calling read() without checking with available(): it returns -1 when there is no data.

concepts.definition: A variable type that holds a single character; its value is written with single quotes and it is case-sensitive.
concepts.example: The check if (c == 'A') is true only when a capital A arrives.
concepts.pitfall: Writing "A" instead of 'A', or comparing with a small 'a' and expecting a capital A.

concepts.definition: Reads the next whole number coming from the serial port and gives it as an int; it skips characters that are not digits.
concepts.example: When B3 arrives, after 'B' has been read, parseInt() returns 3.
concepts.pitfall: Reading the number with read(): you get the character code, not the value of the digit.

concepts.definition: The job of splitting incoming text into meaningful parts such as a command and a number.
concepts.example: In the text B3, B is the command and 3 is the number of blinks.
concepts.pitfall: Not taking the line-ending character into account; it is a byte too and waits to be read.

options: A, B, C and D on four separate lines
ABC on the first line, D on the second line
quiz.explanation: print does not end the line: A and B are written, and println("C") adds C to the same line and closes the line (ABC). println("D") writes D on a new line. For four separate lines, all of them would need to be println.
parseInt() gives 4, so the loop runs 4 times. Each pass takes 150 + 100 = 250 ms. The total is 4 × 250 = 1000 ms.

Capital and small letters are different characters: the incoming 'A' is not equal to 'a'. The condition should be if (c == 'A'). The other lines are correct: available() checks whether there is data and read() takes a single character.

quiz.prompt: If Serial.available() is 0, what does it mean?
options: The serial port has not been opened
No bytes are waiting to be read
quiz.explanation: available() gives the number of bytes in the buffer waiting to be read; 0 only says there is no data to read right now. Calling read() in this case would return -1. A wrong baud rate is a separate problem and does not change this number.

quiz.prompt: The code says Serial.begin(9600); but 115200 is selected in the real Serial Monitor. What do you see on the screen?
options: Nothing, and the board gets damaged
The text scrolls twice as fast
quiz.explanation: When the two sides talk at different speeds, the bytes are misread and meaningless characters appear on the screen. This wrong setting does not damage the board; making the speeds equal solves the problem. The lab matches the two speeds by itself; in a real monitor you match them.
